question: Which radiographic label corresponds to the narrow central shaft of a long bone on an AP humerus film?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: Diaphysis denotes the shaft of a long bone; on the humerus AP film it is the narrow central portion forming the long axis.
Epiphysis is the rounded end forming part of a joint; it would be at the humeral head or distal condyle, not the shaft.
Metaphysis is the flaring zone between shaft and end; it would be adjacent to the epiphysis, not the central shaft.
Greater tubercle is a proximal humeral landmark on the head, not the shaft; it would be correct only if the question asked for a proximal tubercular prominence.
Surgical neck is a proximal narrowing below the humeral head; it is not the long bone shaft itself and would be correct only if the stem asked for the proximal constriction.

question: Choose the phrase that best defines an orthogonal pair of radiographic views.
cited_learning_objective: Define orthogonal radiographic views

options.rationale: Orthogonal views are taken at right angles to one another (e.g., AP and lateral), which provides complementary perspectives.
Views from the same angle are redundant; to be orthogonal they must be perpendicular, so this would be correct only if the views were rotated 90°.
Identical projections are not orthogonal; orthogonal requires differing, perpendicular projections.
Different exposure does not define orthogonality; only geometric angle between projections matters.
Oblique views are angled but not necessarily perpendicular; they are orthogonal only if one is perpendicular to the other.

question: On a pediatric AP pelvis film, which radiographic feature indicates the presence of growth plates?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Epiphyseal plates appearing as radiolucent lines
options.rationale: Pediatric films show physes (epiphyseal plates) as lucent lines between epiphysis and metaphysis; the lecture highlights arrows marking these plates.
Cortical thickening is not a sign of growth plates; growth plates are lucent lines, so this would be correct only if lucency were described.
Fusion indicates skeletal maturity; in children the epiphyseal plate is unfused, so this option would be correct only in an adult film.
SI joint widening is unrelated to physes; it would be correct only if the question targeted SI joint pathology.
Calcified islands are not the typical radiographic appearance of physes; physes appear as radiolucent lines unless abnormal calcification is present.

question: Which term best describes the location on an appendage closer to its attachment to the torso?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the meaning of the terms “proximal” and “distal” as applied to locations in the appendicular skeleton

options.rationale: Proximal denotes nearer the point of attachment of an appendage to the trunk; the lecture defines proximal versus distal along the limb axis.
Distal means farther from the trunk; it would be correct only if the stem asked for the farther location along the appendage.
Medial refers to toward the midline, not distance from the trunk; it would be correct only if the question asked about midline relation.
Lateral denotes away from the midline, not proximity to the torso; it would be correct only for side-to-midline relationships.
Superficial describes depth relative to the surface, not position along the limb; it would be correct only if depth were asked.

question: A child falls and has focal tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Which carpal bone is most likely injured on the wrist PA film?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The scaphoid is the most frequently fractured carpal bone and is associated with anatomical snuffbox tenderness; the lecture highlights this association.
Lunate injuries cause different clinical signs; this would be correct only if the tenderness localized to the central wrist rather than the snuffbox.
Triquetrum fractures present dorsally and are less associated with snuffbox tenderness; it would be correct only with dorsal ulnar-sided pain.
Pisiform is a sesamoid on the ulnar side and not typically tender in snuffbox injuries; it would be correct only if ulnar-palmar pain were present.
Capitate lies centrally and is not linked to snuffbox tenderness; it would be correct only if central wrist pain and radiographic findings pointed to it.

question: Which AP shoulder projection landmark is the rounded structure that articulates with the glenoid?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The humeral head is the rounded proximal humerus that articulates with the glenoid; the lecture labels this on AP shoulder films.
Greater tubercle is a lateral prominence adjacent to the head; it would be correct only if the question asked for a tubercular landmark.
Coracoid is a scapular projection, not the articulating rounded humeral structure; it would be correct only if scapular anatomy were queried.
Acromion is a scapular roof over the joint, not the humeral articulating surface; it would be correct only for scapular landmarks.
Glenoid rim is the scapular socket, not the rounded humeral articulating surface; it would be correct only if the socket were asked.

question: Which pair of views is the classic orthogonal set for evaluating most long-bone injuries?
cited_learning_objective: Define orthogonal radiographic views

options.rationale: AP and lateral are perpendicular projections commonly used as orthogonal views to increase exam sensitivity, as emphasized in the lecture.
PA and oblique are not necessarily perpendicular; they are useful views but not the standard orthogonal AP-lateral pair.
Axillary and AP can be orthogonal for the shoulder specifically, but AP and lateral are the general classic orthogonal pair for long bones.
Oblique and lateral may be complementary but are not the standard orthogonal AP-lateral pair; they would be orthogonal only if taken at right angles.
AP and oblique are angled relative to each other but not the prototypical perpendicular pair; they are used when additional detail is needed.

question: A toddler lands awkwardly and radiographs show a tibial fracture on the lateral view but not on the AP. What principle explains this discrepancy?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.rationale: Superimposition on one projection can obscure nondisplaced fractures; obtaining orthogonal views reduces this limitation and increases sensitivity.

options.text: AP views always miss pediatric fractures
options.rationale: AP views do not always miss fractures; they can miss some due to projection and superimposition, so this would be correct only if AP were inherently insensitive, which is not stated.

options.text: Lateral views use higher exposure revealing fractures
options.rationale: Exposure differences are not the lecture's reason; the lecture attributes detection differences to projection geometry and superimposition.

options.text: Fractures are only visible when displaced inferiorly
options.rationale: Visibility depends on projection, not displacement direction; this would be correct only if the fracture orientation aligned with the projection.

options.text: Pediatric bones are radiolucent so AP fails
options.rationale: Pediatric bones are not uniformly radiolucent; the lecture cites superimposition and nondisplaced fractures as causes of missed findings.

question: Which radiographic view is orthogonal to an AP shoulder and useful to assess glenohumeral articulation?
cited_learning_objective: Define orthogonal radiographic views

options.rationale: The axillary view is perpendicular to the AP shoulder and shows the humeral head–glenoid relationship; the lecture lists it as an orthogonal shoulder view.
PA wrist is unrelated anatomically and not orthogonal to AP shoulder; it would be correct only in a wrist-focused question.
Frog-leg lateral is a hip lateral projection, not the orthogonal partner for AP shoulder.
Oblique foot views are for the foot and not orthogonal to AP shoulder; this would be correct only if the stem asked about foot imaging.
Lateral knee is unrelated to shoulder imaging; it would be correct only for knee assessment.

question: A patient presents after a fall on an outstretched hand with elbow pain. Which fracture is most commonly seen in adults from this mechanism and should be sought on AP and lateral elbow films?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: Radial head fractures commonly result from FOOSH and are the most frequent adult elbow fracture per the lecture; AP and lateral views help detect them.
Olecranon fractures occur from direct trauma or avulsion; this would be correct only if the mechanism and exam localized to the posterior elbow.
Medial epicondyle fractures are more common in children and with valgus stress; it would be correct only with pediatric history or specific exam findings.
Coronoid fractures can accompany dislocation but are less common as isolated FOOSH injuries; it would be correct only with radiographic coronoid disruption.
Supracondylar fractures are common in children after FOOSH, not adults; it would be correct only in a pediatric vignette.

question: Which statement best explains why obtaining at least two orthogonal views increases diagnostic accuracy for skeletal radiographs?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: Perpendicular projections reveal different fracture orientations
options.rationale: Orthogonal views show structures from different angles so fractures aligned with one projection may be visible on the perpendicular view, increasing sensitivity.

options.text: Two views double the exposure improving contrast
options.rationale: Increased exposure is not the lecture's rationale; the benefit arises from geometric perspective, not simply exposure.
Two views reduce but do not eliminate superimposition; more views may be needed for complex anatomy, so this would be correct only if complete elimination were possible.

options.text: They are required to measure bone density accurately
options.rationale: Plain films are limited for bone density assessment; orthogonal views are for structural evaluation, not precise densitometry.

options.text: They allow visualization of soft tissues better
options.rationale: Plain films provide limited soft tissue information; orthogonal views primarily improve bony assessment, so this would be correct only with additional modalities.

question: A shoulder AP film shows complete loss of contact between the humeral head and glenoid. Which diagnosis does this radiographic finding represent?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: Dislocation denotes complete loss of articular contact; the lecture states that dislocation represents complete loss of contact between articular surfaces.
Subluxation is partial loss of contact; this would be correct only if partial, not complete, separation were present.
A glenoid rim fracture may accompany dislocation but does not by itself define complete loss of contact; it would be correct only with radiographic rim disruption.
Rotator cuff tears are soft-tissue injuries not diagnosed by loss of joint contact on plain film; this would be correct only with MRI or clinical correlation.
AC separation affects the acromioclavicular articulation, not the glenohumeral contact; it would be correct only if the AC joint were widened on film.

question: Which hip fracture type and femoral landmark pairing are important to distinguish in elderly patients because both are common?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The lecture notes femoral neck and intertrochanteric fractures as the two most common hip fractures in elderly patients and emphasizes distinguishing them.
Greater trochanter avulsions and acetabular rim fractures are different entities; this would be correct only if those were the two most common types, which the lecture does not state.
Lesser trochanter injuries and shaft fractures occur but are not listed as the two most common hip fractures in the elderly; it would be correct only with different epidemiology.
Femoral head fractures and pubic ramus fractures are distinct; this pairing is not the common elderly hip fracture pair described in the lecture.

Intertrochanteric crest involvement may occur with intertrochanteric fractures, but acetabular fractures are a separate category; this would be correct only if acetabular fractures were equally common.

question: A lateral knee film shows a transverse disruption through the patella with visible fragments. Which statement best describes the value of orthogonal views in this case?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: Fracture may be more obvious on lateral than AP
options.rationale: The lecture illustrates that some fractures (e.g., patella) are more conspicuous on lateral views, demonstrating the diagnostic value of orthogonal imaging.

options.text: AP view always shows patellar fragments better
options.rationale: AP does not always show patellar fragments better; lateral often reveals displacement, so this would be correct only if AP provided superior visualization.

options.text: Two views are unnecessary if one shows fragments
options.rationale: Even if one view shows fragments, orthogonal views help assess displacement and fragment relationships; this would be correct only if management did not require additional perspective.

options.text: Lateral view eliminates need for CT in all cases
options.rationale: Lateral films improve detection but do not universally replace CT for complex fractures; it would be correct only if the lecture stated CT was never needed.

options.text: AP and lateral views are redundant for patella
options.rationale: They are complementary rather than redundant; this would be correct only if both views provided identical information, which is not the case.

question: Which carpal bone sequence mnemonic corresponds to the proximal row from radial to ulnar on a PA wrist film?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The lecture presents the mnemonic 'So Long To Pinky' for the proximal row: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform on PA wrist films.
Those are the distal row carpal bones; this would be correct only if the distal row were asked.
This lists distal row bones in radial-to-ulnar order but not the proximal row; it would be correct for distal row identification.
This order is incorrect for the proximal row; it would be correct only if the bones were rearranged to the proper radial-to-ulnar sequence.
This mixes distal and proximal bones and is not the proximal row sequence; it would be correct only with a different mnemonic.

question: A patient with shoulder trauma has an AP film showing the humeral head displaced anteriorly relative to the glenoid. Which clinical interpretation aligns with this radiographic relationship?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: Anterior displacement of the humeral head relative to the glenoid indicates an anterior dislocation; the lecture notes anterior dislocation examples and loss of articular contact.
Posterior dislocation would show posterior displacement of the humeral head; this would be correct only if the head lay posterior to the glenoid.
AC separation affects the acromioclavicular articulation, not humeral head–glenoid alignment; it would be correct only with AC joint widening on film.
A nondisplaced proximal humeral fracture would not show humeral head displacement relative to the glenoid; it would be correct only if fracture lines were present without displacement.
Rotator cuff arthropathy involves chronic joint changes and superior migration, not acute anterior displacement; it would be correct only with chronic radiographic features.

question: Which femoral landmark is described as the flaring portion between the shaft and the end of a long bone?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize the epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of a long bone on a radiograph

options.rationale: Metaphysis is the flaring zone between diaphysis and epiphysis; the lecture defines it as the flaring portion of a long bone.
Diaphysis is the central shaft, not the flaring portion; it would be correct only if the stem asked for the shaft.
Epiphysis is the rounded end forming part of a joint, not the flaring metaphyseal region; it would be correct only for the bone end.
Apophysis is a secondary ossification site for tendon attachment and is not the metaphyseal flaring zone; it would be correct only if tendon attachment ossification were asked.
Periosteum is the bone covering, not a bony region like metaphysis; it would be correct only in a question about bone coverings.

question: A radiograph of the ankle shows a fracture at the lateral malleolus. Which bone is fractured?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The lateral malleolus is the distal fibula; the lecture labels lateral malleolus as the fibular distal prominence.
The distal tibia forms the medial malleolus, not the lateral; this would be correct only if the medial malleolus were fractured.
Talus is an ankle bone articulating with tibia and fibula; it is not the lateral malleolus, so this would be correct only with talar fracture evidence.
Calcaneus is the heel bone and not the lateral malleolus; it would be correct only if the heel were fractured.
Navicular is a midfoot bone, not the lateral malleolus; it would be correct only in a midfoot injury scenario.

question: A patient falls and has focal tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal. Which standard foot radiographic view set should be obtained to evaluate this area?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: Standard foot radiographs include AP, oblique, and lateral views to assess metatarsal and tarsal injuries, as listed in the lecture.
PA wrist views are for the wrist, not the foot; this would be correct only if the injury were in the wrist.
AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral are hip/pelvis views, not standard foot views; they would be correct only for proximal femur assessment.
Axillary shoulder views are for the shoulder; they are unrelated to foot imaging and would be correct only in shoulder trauma.
AP tibia-fibula films evaluate the leg bones but not the foot; this would be correct only if the question targeted tibial or fibular injury.

question: A lateral ankle film demonstrates a transverse fracture through the distal fibula with minimal displacement. The AP view appears normal. What is the most likely explanation based on radiographic principles?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: Fracture plane aligned with AP projection
options.rationale: If the fracture plane is parallel to the AP beam, it may be occult on AP but visible on lateral; orthogonal views reveal different orientations.

options.text: Lateral view uses magnification revealing tiny fractures
options.rationale: Magnification is not the lecture's explanation; projection geometry and alignment of the fracture with the beam account for visibility differences.

options.text: AP film was underexposed causing nondetection
options.rationale: Exposure issues are not the primary reason cited; the lecture emphasizes projection and superimposition rather than exposure differences.

options.text: Fibular fractures are only visible on lateral views
options.rationale: Fibular fractures can be seen on AP or lateral depending on orientation; this would be correct only if the fracture orientation consistently favored lateral imaging.

options.text: Ankle fractures displace only in sagittal plane
options.rationale: Fracture displacement can occur in multiple planes; this statement is too absolute and would be correct only with specific fracture mechanics.

question: Which labeled region of a long bone forms part of a joint and is typically rounded on radiographs?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize the epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of a long bone on a radiograph

options.rationale: Epiphysis is the end part of a long bone, rounded and forming part of a joint, as defined in the lecture.
Diaphysis is the shaft and not the rounded joint-forming end; it would be correct only if the shaft were asked.
Metaphysis is the flaring region between shaft and end, not the rounded articular end; it would be correct only if flaring were queried.
Periarticular cortex refers to cortical bone near a joint but is not the epiphyseal rounded end; it would be correct only in a cortical-focused question.
Growth plate (physis) lies between epiphysis and metaphysis and is not the rounded articular epiphysis itself; it would be correct only if the physis were the target.

question: A radiograph shows a widened acromioclavicular joint with inferior displacement of the acromion relative to the clavicle. Which diagnosis does this describe?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: Widened AC joint and inferior displacement of the acromion indicate acromioclavicular separation, as shown in the lecture comparison images.
Midshaft clavicle fractures show shaft discontinuity rather than AC joint widening; this would be correct only with a visible midshaft fracture.
Glenohumeral dislocation involves humeral head–glenoid alignment, not AC joint widening; it would be correct only with loss of glenohumeral contact.
Sternoclavicular dislocation affects the medial clavicle at the sternum, not the AC joint; it would be correct only with medial clavicular displacement.
Osteolysis causes bone resorption, not acute AC joint widening with acromial displacement; it would be correct only with chronic radiographic changes.

question: Which radiographic landmark on an AP femur film corresponds to the lateral prominence near the proximal femur?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The greater trochanter is the lateral proximal femoral prominence labeled on AP femur films in the lecture.
Lesser trochanter is a medial/posteromedial prominence, not the lateral one; it would be correct only if medial prominence were asked.
Intertrochanteric crest is a posterior ridge between trochanters, not the lateral prominence; it would be correct only on posterior views.
Femoral head is the rounded articular surface, not the lateral trochanteric prominence; it would be correct only if the articulating surface were queried.
Femoral neck is the constricted region distal to the head, not the lateral trochanter; it would be correct only if the neck were the target.

question: A patient with wrist trauma has a normal AP film but persistent snuffbox tenderness. Which next step is most consistent with the lecture's emphasis on imaging strategy?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: Obtain additional views including scaphoid-specific projections
options.rationale: Because scaphoid fractures can be occult on standard AP films, the lecture recommends additional views (and orthogonal perspectives) to increase detection.

options.text: Accept normal AP and discharge without follow-up
options.rationale: Discharging after a normal AP ignores the lecture's point that nondisplaced fractures may be missed; this would be correct only with no clinical concern.

options.text: Order immediate MRI for all wrist injuries
options.rationale: MRI is more sensitive but the lecture emphasizes obtaining orthogonal and targeted radiographic views first; MRI would be correct only if radiographs and clinical suspicion warranted advanced imaging.

options.text: Immobilize and repeat AP in 6 weeks only
options.rationale: Delayed radiographs can show healing but the lecture suggests obtaining orthogonal and targeted views initially; waiting without additional views is not the recommended immediate step.

options.text: Perform only a lateral wrist radiograph
options.rationale: A single lateral may still miss scaphoid fractures; the lecture advocates multiple views including scaphoid-specific projections rather than a lone lateral.

question: Which region of a long bone is directly adjacent to the growth plate and flares toward the shaft?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize the epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of a long bone on a radiograph

options.rationale: Metaphysis lies between the epiphysis and diaphysis and flares toward the shaft; the lecture defines it as the flaring portion.
Epiphysis is the end part adjacent to the growth plate but is the articular end rather than the flaring metaphyseal zone; it would be correct only if the end itself were asked.
Diaphysis is the central shaft, not the flaring region adjacent to the physis; it would be correct only for shaft identification.
Physis (growth plate) is the cartilaginous line between epiphysis and metaphysis, not the metaphyseal flare itself; it would be correct only if the growth plate were targeted.
Cancellous bone is trabecular bone present in many regions but is not the specific metaphyseal flaring zone; it would be correct only in a histologic context.

question: A radiograph of the forearm shows the radial styloid process laterally and the ulnar styloid medially on the AP view. Which statement correctly describes their orientation?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Radial styloid is lateral; ulnar styloid is medial
options.rationale: On AP forearm films, the radial styloid lies laterally and the ulnar styloid medially; the lecture labels these landmarks accordingly.

options.text: Radial styloid is medial; ulnar styloid is lateral
options.rationale: This reverses the orientation; it would be correct only if the film were mirrored or the limb reversed.
They are on opposite sides of the wrist; this would be correct only in an abnormal anatomic variant not discussed in the lecture.
They are not both medial; this would be correct only with a mirrored image or labeling error.

options.text: Styloid orientation cannot be determined on AP
options.rationale: AP films show lateral-medial relationships, so orientation can be determined; this would be correct only if the film were rotated or poorly positioned.

question: A patient presents after a fall with knee pain. Lateral knee radiograph shows a displaced transverse patellar fracture. Which management-relevant detail is best assessed on the lateral view?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: Lateral views often show patellar fragment displacement and relationships clearly, which is important for management decisions; the lecture highlights lateral utility.
Plateau depression is better seen on AP or dedicated tibial plateau views; this would be correct only if the plateau were specifically imaged.
ACL is a soft-tissue structure not assessed on plain films; this would be correct only with MRI or clinical testing.
Tendon tears are soft-tissue injuries and may be inferred from fragment displacement but are not directly visualized on plain film; this would be correct only with adjunct imaging.
Cartilage loss is not well assessed on radiographs; this would be correct only with advanced imaging or chronic degenerative changes.

question: Which anatomical term describes a bone region that is the rounded articular end and often contains the growth plate in children?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize the epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of a long bone on a radiograph

options.rationale: Epiphysis is the rounded end forming part of a joint and is adjacent to the physis in pediatric films, as described in the lecture.
Metaphysis flares between shaft and end but is not the rounded articular end; it would be correct only if flaring were the focus.
Diaphysis is the shaft and not the articular end; it would be correct only for shaft identification.
Physis is the growth plate itself, not the epiphyseal bone end; it would be correct only if the growth plate were the target.
Apophysis is a secondary ossification center for tendon attachment, not the primary rounded articular epiphysis; it would be correct only in tendon-attachment contexts.

question: A radiograph shows a midshaft clavicular discontinuity in a young adult. Which location along the clavicle is most commonly fractured according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: Clavicular fractures most commonly occur in the midshaft in children and young adults, as stated in the lecture.
Medial clavicle fractures are less common; this would be correct only if the epidemiology favored medial injuries.
Lateral clavicle fractures occur but are less common than midshaft fractures; it would be correct only with lateral trauma patterns.
AC joint injuries involve the acromioclavicular articulation rather than a clavicular midshaft fracture; it would be correct only if the AC joint were disrupted.
Sternoclavicular injuries affect the medial articulation, not the common midshaft fracture site; it would be correct only with medial displacement.

question: A patient has a suspected toddler tibial fracture after a fall. The AP film is negative but the lateral shows a subtle cortical break. Which teaching point from the lecture best explains the imaging approach?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: Obtain at least two orthogonal views to increase sensitivity
options.rationale: The lecture emphasizes getting at least two orthogonal views in nearly all cases because sensitivity and accuracy improve and some fractures are only visible on one projection.

options.text: Single AP view is sufficient for tibial fractures
options.rationale: A single AP is often insufficient; this would be correct only if the fracture orientation always favored AP, which the lecture contradicts.

options.text: Lateral views are unnecessary in children
options.rationale: The lecture does not recommend omitting lateral views in children; this would be correct only if lateral views added no diagnostic value.

options.text: CT should replace radiographs for all tibial injuries
options.rationale: CT is more sensitive but the lecture supports plain films as first-line with orthogonal views; CT would be correct only when radiographs are inconclusive.

options.text: Stress fractures are always visible on AP
options.rationale: Stress fractures may be occult on plain films; this statement is incorrect and would be correct only with advanced imaging or later healing changes.

question: Which term describes the bone region that is the primary weight-bearing shaft visible on an AP tibia-fibula film?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize the epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of a long bone on a radiograph

options.rationale: Diaphysis refers to the shaft of a long bone (e.g., tibial diaphysis) and is the primary long-axis weight-bearing region on AP films.
Epiphysis is the end part forming joints, not the shaft; it would be correct only if the joint end were the focus.
Metaphysis is the flaring zone near the ends, not the central shaft; it would be correct only if the flaring region were asked.
Medullary canal is the internal cavity within the diaphysis, not the external shaft region named diaphysis; it would be correct only in an internal-structure question.
Cortical rim describes the dense outer bone but is not the anatomical region name like diaphysis; it would be correct only in a cortical-focused stem.

question: A radiograph of the pelvis shows the acetabulum, femoral head, and femoral neck. Which of these is the articular socket that receives the femoral head?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The acetabulum is the pelvic socket that articulates with the femoral head; the lecture labels the acetabulum on AP pelvis films.
Femoral neck connects head to shaft but is not the socket; it would be correct only if the question asked for the femoral connection region.
Greater trochanter is a lateral prominence, not the acetabular socket; it would be correct only for lateral femoral landmarks.
Ischial tuberosity is a pelvic landmark inferior to the acetabulum and not the socket; it would be correct only in a different pelvic anatomy question.
Pubic symphysis is the midline pelvic joint, not the acetabular socket; it would be correct only if midline pelvic anatomy were asked.

question: A patient with ankle trauma has tenderness over the medial malleolus. Which bone and specific malleolus should be carefully evaluated on AP and lateral ankle films?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The medial malleolus is the distal tibia; the lecture labels the medial malleolus as the tibial distal prominence to evaluate on ankle films.
Lateral malleolus is the distal fibula and would be evaluated for lateral tenderness, not medial; it would be correct only with lateral pain.
Talus articulates with malleoli but is not the medial malleolus; it would be correct only if talar injury were suspected.
Sustentaculum tali is a calcaneal shelf, not the medial malleolus; it would be correct only in hindfoot injury contexts.
Navicular is a midfoot bone and not the medial malleolus; it would be correct only with midfoot pain.

question: A patient presents with shoulder pain after a fall. AP and axillary views show the humeral head completely separated from the glenoid. Which immediate interpretation and next imaging principle follows the lecture guidance?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Confirm dislocation and obtain orthogonal views to assess associated fractures
options.rationale: Complete loss of contact indicates dislocation; the lecture emphasizes orthogonal views (e.g., AP and axillary) to evaluate alignment and associated bony injury.

options.text: Label as rotator cuff tear and schedule MRI only
options.rationale: Rotator cuff tears are soft-tissue injuries not diagnosed by loss of articular contact; MRI may be useful but orthogonal radiographs are first-line for dislocation assessment.

options.text: Reduce without further imaging since AP shows dislocation
options.rationale: Reduction decisions often require orthogonal views to assess associated fractures; proceeding without full radiographic assessment risks missing fractures.

options.text: Order only a CT scan and skip plain films
options.rationale: CT can be helpful but plain films with orthogonal views are first-line per the lecture; CT would be correct only if radiographs were inconclusive.
AC separation affects the acromioclavicular joint, not glenohumeral dislocation; this would be correct only with AC joint widening on films.

question: Which anatomical descriptor applies to the bone segment located farther from the torso along an arm or leg?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the meaning of the terms “proximal” and “distal” as applied to locations in the appendicular skeleton

options.rationale: Distal denotes a location farther from the point of attachment of an appendage to the torso; the lecture defines distal in contrast to proximal.
Proximal means nearer the torso; this would be correct only if the stem asked for the nearer location.
Medial refers to toward the midline, not distance from the torso; it would be correct only in a midline relation question.
Superficial describes depth relative to the surface, not position along the limb; it would be correct only for depth descriptors.
Contralateral means on the opposite side of the body, not distal; it would be correct only in a side-to-side comparison.

question: A radiograph of the hand labels proximal, intermediate, and distal phalanges. Which phalanx is nearest the fingertip?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The distal phalanx is the bone nearest the fingertip; the lecture diagrams distal, intermediate, and proximal phalanges.
Proximal phalanx is nearest the hand, not the fingertip; it would be correct only if the base of the finger were asked.
Intermediate (middle) phalanx lies between proximal and distal and is absent in the thumb; it would be correct only for middle phalanx identification.
Metacarpals form the hand skeleton proximal to the phalanges, not the fingertip; it would be correct only in a hand-base question.
Sesamoids are small bones near tendons (e.g., thumb) and are not the distal phalanx; this would be correct only in a tendon-related context.

question: A radiograph shows the femoral head, neck, and greater trochanter. Which of these is closest to the trunk and thus considered proximal?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the meaning of the terms “proximal” and “distal” as applied to locations in the appendicular skeleton

options.rationale: The femoral head is the most proximal of the listed landmarks, articulating with the acetabulum and closest to the trunk along the limb axis.
Greater trochanter is lateral and slightly distal to the head; it would be correct only if asked for a lateral prominence rather than the most proximal structure.
Femoral neck lies between head and shaft and is distal to the head; it would be correct only if the neck were the target.
Lesser trochanter is more distal/posteromedial than the head; it would be correct only in a different proximal-distal comparison.
Diaphysis is the shaft and is distal to the proximal landmarks listed; it would be correct only if the shaft were asked.

question: A patient falls and has focal tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox but initial radiographs are inconclusive. Which anatomical bone and clinical sign pairing from the lecture supports high suspicion for occult fracture?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The lecture states scaphoid is most frequently fractured and that focal tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is a sign of scaphoid fracture, supporting further targeted imaging.
Lunate is central and not classically associated with snuffbox tenderness; this would be correct only if clinical findings localized to the lunate region.
Triquetrum lies ulnarly and is not typically tender in the snuffbox; it would be correct only with ulnar-sided dorsal pain.
Capitate is central and not linked to snuffbox tenderness; it would be correct only with central wrist pain and radiographic evidence.
Pisiform is ulnar-palmar and not in the snuffbox; it would be correct only with ulnar-palmar tenderness.

question: Which imaging principle from the lecture justifies obtaining more than two views for areas of complex anatomy?
cited_learning_objective: Define orthogonal radiographic views

options.text: Complex anatomy may require >2 views to avoid superimposition
options.rationale: The lecture notes that some complex anatomical regions need more than two views to adequately evaluate because superimposed structures can obscure pathology.

options.text: More views always reduce radiation dose
options.rationale: Additional views increase diagnostic information but do not reduce dose; this would be correct only in a context where fewer repeats were needed overall.

options.text: Three views are required for all joints
options.rationale: The lecture recommends at least two orthogonal views and more for complex areas, not a universal three-view rule; this would be correct only for specific joints.
Oblique views complement but do not universally replace orthogonal views; this would be correct only if oblique provided the necessary perpendicular perspective.

options.text: Additional views are only for soft tissues
options.rationale: Additional views are primarily for bony evaluation in complex anatomy; this would be correct only if soft-tissue assessment were the goal.

question: A lateral forearm film labels the radial head, radial neck, and capitulum. Which articulation does the capitulum form with on the AP elbow film?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: The capitulum articulates with the radial head; the lecture uses the mnemonic 'Cap on head' to illustrate this relationship.
Olecranon is part of the ulna articulating with the trochlea, not the capitulum; it would be correct only for ulnohumeral articulation.
Coronoid process articulates with the trochlea region, not the capitulum; it would be correct only with trochlear involvement.
Medial epicondyle is a humeral prominence, not the articulating surface for the radial head; it would be correct only in a different anatomical question.
Lateral epicondyle is a humeral landmark near the capitulum but is not the articulating surface; it would be correct only if the question asked for a prominence.

question: A radiograph of the foot labels cuneiforms, navicular, and cuboid. Which set of bones are the cuneiforms classified as?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: Cuneiforms are tarsal bones in the midfoot; the lecture lists tarsal bones including the cuneiforms.
Metatarsals are distal to tarsals and form the forefoot; this would be correct only if the bones were the long metatarsal bones.
Phalanges are toe bones distal to metatarsals, not cuneiforms; it would be correct only in a phalangeal question.
Sesamoids are small bones near tendons (e.g., under the first metatarsal head), not cuneiforms; it would be correct only in a tendon-related context.
Calcaneus is the heel bone and not the cuneiforms; this would be correct only in hindfoot anatomy.

question: A patient has a displaced intertrochanteric femur fracture on AP hip film. Which anatomic region listed in the lecture does this fracture involve?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.rationale: Intertrochanteric fractures occur between the greater and lesser trochanters; the lecture highlights this region as distinct from femoral neck fractures.
Femoral head fractures involve the articular surface, not the intertrochanteric region; this would be correct only with head involvement.
Diaphyseal midshaft fractures are distal to the intertrochanteric region; this would be correct only with shaft fracture evidence.
Acetabular rim is pelvic, not femoral; it would be correct only if the pelvis were fractured.
Lesser trochanter may be involved but intertrochanteric fractures span between trochanters; this would be correct only if the lesser trochanter were isolatedly fractured.

question: A clinician asks why plain films remain useful despite limited soft-tissue information. Which lecture point best supports continuing to use skeletal radiographs as first-line after trauma?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Plain films are inexpensive and readily available
options.rationale: The lecture states that plain films are inexpensive and readily available, making them first-line for initial skeletal trauma evaluation despite soft-tissue limitations.

options.text: Plain films detect all early infections and tumors
options.rationale: The lecture notes limited sensitivity for early tumor or infection; this statement would be correct only if plain films were highly sensitive for those conditions.

options.text: Plain films replace MRI for soft tissues
options.rationale: Plain films provide little soft-tissue information and do not replace MRI; this would be correct only if soft-tissue detail were adequate on radiographs.

options.text: Plain films always show nondisplaced fractures
options.rationale: Nondisplaced fractures may be occult on radiographs; this would be correct only if radiographs had perfect sensitivity.

options.text: Plain films are the most sensitive modality for stress fractures
options.rationale: The lecture indicates limited sensitivity for stress fractures; this option would be correct only with advanced imaging like MRI.
